```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
```

MNLFAic tests for differential item functioning (DIF) with respect to an
arbitrary number of continuous or categorical person covariates, without
pre-specified anchor items, and lets item covariates explain part of the DIF.
For example, some mathematics items might be harder for English learners than
others, and part of that difference might be explained by how much reading each
item requires. The package fits a two-parameter logistic moderated nonlinear
factor analysis with item covariates (MNLFA-IC) and reports:

- **impact**: differences in the mean and variance of the latent trait
  associated with each person covariate;
- **item-covariate effects**: how DIF depends on the characteristics of the
  items;
- **residual DIF**: item-specific DIF that the item covariates do not explain,
  with hypothesis tests.

No items need to be specified as DIF-free a priori. Instead, the model is
identified by assuming that residual DIF is sparse. `vignette("method", package = "MNLFAic")`
describes the model and the procedure.

```{r}
library(MNLFAic)
```

## Example data

We simulate a 30-item mathematics test taken by 1,000 students. Person
covariates are English-learner status (`el`, 0/1) and grade (3 to 5, centered
at grade 4). Item covariates are each item's reading load (`reading`, the
number of words in the item) and content area (`domain`: number, geometry or
data).

```{r}
set.seed(4)
N <- 1000; J <- 30
persons <- data.frame(el = rbinom(N, 1, 0.3),
                      grade = sample(3:5, N, replace = TRUE) - 4)
items <- data.frame(item = sprintf("item%02d", 1:J),
                    reading = round(runif(J, 10, 80)),
                    domain = rep(c("number", "geometry", "data"), length.out = J))
head(items)
```

The simulated truth:

- **impact on the mean:** English learners are 0.4 SD lower, and each grade
  adds 0.5 SD;
- **impact on the variance:** the log-variance rises by 0.2 per grade (the SD
  grows by about 10% per grade); English learners and other students are
  equally variable;
- **DIF explained by item covariates:** each SD of reading load makes an item
  0.3 SD harder for English learners; geometry items become 0.25 SD easier per
  grade than the average item, number items 0.25 SD harder, and data items are
  no different;
- **residual DIF:** four items have item-specific DIF, two for English-learner
  status and two for grade.

`simulate_mnlfa_ic()` codes the item covariates by the same rules as the
analysis (see below), so the effects refer to the coded columns.

```{r}
effects <- matrix(0, 3, 2,
                  dimnames = list(c("reading", "domain_data", "domain_geometry"),
                                  c("el", "grade")))
effects["reading", "el"] <- 0.3
effects["domain_geometry", "grade"] <- -0.25
residual <- matrix(0, J, 2)
residual[c(5, 18), 1] <- c(0.6, -0.5)
residual[c(11, 26), 2] <- c(0.4, -0.4)

sim <- simulate_mnlfa_ic(persons, ~ el + grade, items, ~ reading + domain,
                         slopes = round(runif(J, 0.8, 2), 2),
                         intercepts = round(rnorm(J), 2),
                         impact = c(-0.4, 0.5), variance_impact = c(0, 0.2),
                         effects = effects, residual_dif = residual,
                         item_omit = list(domain = "number"), seed = 1)
responses <- sim$responses
dim(responses)
```

## Fitting the model

```{r}
fit <- mnlfa_ic(responses, person_data = persons, person = ~ el + grade,
                item_data = items, item = ~ reading + domain,
                control = mnlfa_control(item_omit = list(domain = "number"),
                                        M = 2000, seed = 1))
fit
```

The arguments are:

- `responses`: an N x J matrix or data frame of 0/1 responses. Missing
  responses (`NA`) are allowed; they are handled by full-information maximum
  likelihood, which assumes they are missing at random.
- `person_data` and `person`: a data frame with one row per person, and a
  one-sided formula. The formula is expanded without an intercept: numeric
  variables enter as they are, factors as 0/1 dummies, and `a * b` adds the
  product. The person with every covariate at 0 is the reference (latent mean
  0, variance 1), so center continuous covariates yourself if 0 is not a
  meaningful value.
- `item_data` and `item`: a data frame with one row per item, in the order of
  the columns of `responses`, and a one-sided formula. If `item_data` has an
  `item` column, it must match the column names of `responses`. Continuous
  item covariates are centered over items and, by default, standardized, so
  their effects are per SD of the item covariate. Categorical item covariates
  are effect-coded: each category's effect is relative to the average over
  categories, and the effect of the level named in `item_omit` (default: the
  first level) is implied as minus the sum of the others.
- `control`: settings from `mnlfa_control()`. The default number of bootstrap
  draws is `M = 10000`; we use 2,000 here to keep the vignette fast. `seed`
  makes the bootstrap reproducible without changing your own random-number
  stream.

The fit has three stages: a maximum-likelihood fit with DIF free for every
item; a weighted median regression that picks, among the many equivalent
solutions, the one in which residual DIF is sparsest; and a parametric
bootstrap for inference. The print-out reports whether Stage 1 converged.

```{r}
fit$timing
```

## Reading the results

`summary()` collects the main tables.

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

All DIF quantities are on the **difficulty scale**: shifts in item difficulty
in latent-SD units, per unit of the person covariate, with positive values
meaning **harder** for persons with higher values of the covariate (here: for
English learners, or for students in higher grades).

- **Impact on the latent mean**: the English-learner and grade differences in
  mathematics after DIF has been separated out. The intervals are symmetric bootstrap
  intervals.
- **Impact on the latent log-variance**: whether the spread of the latent
  trait depends on the covariates (Wald tests from Stage 1). Here the spread
  grows with grade and does not differ for English learners.
- **Item-covariate effects on DIF**: how DIF depends on the items'
  characteristics. Here each SD of reading load makes an item about 0.27 SD
  harder for English learners, while content area explains grade DIF:
  relative to the average item, geometry items become easier in higher grades
  (about 0.23 SD per grade) and number items harder (about 0.20 SD). The row
  for the omitted category (`domain_number`) is the implied effect, with its
  own interval.
- **Joint tests**: whether a categorical item covariate matters at all for a
  person covariate (a Wald test with the bootstrap covariance; bootstrap and
  chi-square p-values).
- **Impact for an item of each category**: the English-learner or grade
  difference that an item of each category, with no residual DIF, would show.
  Per grade, geometry items would show a larger difference and number items a
  smaller one than the overall impact.
- **Residual DIF flagged**: items whose DIF is not explained by the item
  covariates, flagged by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at a 5% false
  discovery rate across all items and person covariates.
- **Identification margin**: a check of the sparsity assumption (see
  [Checking the identifying assumption](#checking-the-identifying-assumption)).

### Item-level results

`dif_table()` gives one row per item and person covariate, with residual DIF,
its interval and p-values, and the split of total DIF into the part explained
by the item covariates and the residual.

```{r}
dt <- dif_table(fit)
names(dt)
cols <- c("item", "covariate", "est", "ci_low", "ci_high", "p_bh", "flag", "total", "explained",
          "reading", "domain")
num <- sapply(dt, is.numeric)
dt[num] <- round(dt[num], 3)
head(dt[, cols])
dt[dt$flag, cols]
```

Items whose residual DIF is estimated as exactly 0 lie on the fitted plane of
the Stage-2 regression; with no residual DIF, their DIF is entirely explained
by their item covariates.

`dif_table(fit, type = "total")` reports total DIF (explained plus residual)
with its own intervals and p-values instead.

### Extracting estimates

`coef()` and `confint()` return single tables, and `vcov()` the Stage-1
covariance matrix.

```{r}
coef(fit, "impact")
coef(fit, "effects")
confint(fit, "effects")
```

## Checking the identifying assumption

The model is identified by assuming that, for each person covariate, residual
DIF is sparse: the slope-weighted total of absolute residual DIF is smallest at
the true values. Roughly, items with residual DIF must be a minority, and with
a categorical item covariate, roughly a minority within each category.
`diagnose()` reports three checks.

```{r}
diagnose(fit)
```

- **Margin rho**, computed from the cells with unadjusted p < .05: the
  assumption requires rho < 1. Undetected residual DIF makes this plug-in
  value too optimistic, so treat it as a one-sided warning: values above about
  0.4 suggest that intervals for item-covariate effects may be too narrow,
  while a low value is not a guarantee.
- **Tolerance**: how many same-signed residual-DIF items each group of items
  (each category, and the items with the lowest and highest 10% of each
  continuous covariate) could contain before the assumption fails.
- **Design**: correlations of the slopes with the item covariates (high values
  make impact hard to separate from item-covariate DIF), the condition number,
  and the items with the most leverage.

## Without item covariates

With `item = NULL` (the default), the analysis is Chen et al.'s (2023)
anchor-free method, here for an arbitrary number of continuous or categorical
person covariates: impact and item-specific DIF, identified by sparsity of all
DIF.

```{r}
fit0 <- mnlfa_ic(responses, persons, ~ el + grade,
                 control = mnlfa_control(M = 2000, seed = 1))
fit0
```

Without item covariates, DIF that is shared by a group of items (here,
reading-heavy items for English learners, and geometry and number items for
grade) can only be reported item by item. The sparsity assumption then
concerns all DIF rather than residual DIF, and impact refers to a different
reference point. In these data, where most items' DIF follows their reading
load or content area, all DIF is far from sparse, so that assumption is
doubtful.

## Practical notes

- **Run time.** Stage 1 dominates. With 30 items and 1,000 persons it takes a
  few seconds; with 267 items and 1,190 persons about a minute and a half.
  Stage 3 with the default 10,000 draws adds about 10 to 15 seconds at that
  size.
- **Changing inference settings.** `infer()` reruns the bootstrap with new
  settings, reusing the Stage-1 fit, e.g. `infer(fit, M = 10000, seed = 2)` or
  `infer(fit, level = 0.9)`.
- **Sparse items.** Items with very few correct or incorrect responses,
  overall or within a group of a binary person covariate, give a warning:
  their DIF is poorly determined and can destabilize the fit. Consider
  screening out near-ceiling and near-floor items.
- **Missing person covariates.** By default `mnlfa_ic()` stops if any person
  covariate is missing; `na_action = "omit"` drops those persons with a
  message.
- **Convergence.** Check that the print-out says Stage 1 converged. A fit that
  did not converge should not be used for inference.
- **Parameterization.** `mnlfa_control(form = "slope-intercept")` states DIF
  and item-covariate effects as shifts in logits instead of difficulties. With
  item covariates the two forms are different models, not rescalings of each
  other.
- **Clustered persons (experimental).** `cluster = "school"` (a column of
  `person_data`, or a vector) adds a cluster-robust covariance for inference.
- **Checking a fitted model.** `simulate(fit, nsim)` generates data sets from
  the fitted model, which can be analyzed again to check how the procedure
  performs in a design like yours.

## References

Chen, Y., Li, C., Ouyang, J., & Xu, G. (2023). DIF statistical inference
without knowing anchoring items. *Psychometrika, 88*, 1097-1122. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-023-09930-9>
